results.title: Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI)
results.content: Heat exposure for a human depends on the temperature, humidity, wind speed, solar radiation, clothes worn and the intensity of the work. We use two heat indexes: WBGT (wet bulb globe temperature) that has been used for decades and has solid empirical backing; UTCI (Universal Thermal Climate Index) is a modern heat stress index developed from a physiological model. When the body generates heat (by work) faster than it can lose it, the core body temperature rises. * ISO (1989) Hot environments − Estimation of the heat stress on working man, based on the WBGT-index (wet bulb globe temperature). Heat exposure for a human depends on the temperature, humidity, wind speed, solar radiation, clothes worn and the intensity of the work. We use two heat indexes: WBGT (wet bulb globe temperature) that has been used for decades and has solid empirical backing; UTCI (Universal Thermal Climate Index) is a modern heat stress index developed from a physiological model. UTCI is based on the UTCI-Fiala model, which combines a dynamic thermoregulation model of the human body together with a temperature-varying clothing insulation model, both describing distinct states depending on different ambient factors. Altogether, UTCI provides an estimation of the "apparent" temperature that our body would feel under a given environmental condition specified by the air temperature, wind, humidity and radiation. This apparent temperature is in reality the temperature that a reference environment, defined by fixed values of humidity, wind and radiation, should have in order to produce in our body the same physiological reaction of the one produced by the initial given environment. UTCI-Fiala multi-node model of human heat transfer and temperature regulation. It contains assumptions about the human body mass and height, clothing, amount of physical activity, individual heat tolerance, sunlight and ultraviolet radiation exposure, and the wind speed. Significant deviations from these will result in heat index values which do not accurately reflect the perceived temperature. The heat index (HI) is an index that combines air temperature and relative humidity in shaded areas, to suggest a human-perceived equivalent temperature, i.e. what it feels like to the human body. results.title: What is UTCI? | The UTCI story hub
results.content: This estimation of our physiological reaction to the external conditions is what UTCI measures and, as you can see, the difference with the standard measurement of the air temperature can be notable. UTCI is based on the UTCI-Fiala model (Fiala et al., 2012), which combines a dynamic thermoregulation model of the human body together with a temperature-varying clothing insulation model, both describing distinct states depending on different ambient factors. Altogether, UTCI provides an estimation of the “apparent” temperature that our body would feel under a given environmental condition specified by the air temperature, wind, humidity and radiation. ## Does the air temperature differ a lot from the UTCI values? The figure below shows how monthly averages for the maximum daily values of both variables, air temperature and UTCI, change along the year in Barcelona (Spain). Contrary to what happens in Barcelona, during summer in London, daily maximum air temperatures are on average similar to daily maximum UTCI values. The map shows a wildly general pattern of the differences between the annual averages of the daily maximum values of UTCI and air temperature all around the Earth. UTCI values are directly computed from the ERA5 reanalysis fields of air temperature, wind, humidity and radiation providing an hourly temporal resolution in a 0.25° grid coveraging from 60°S to 90°N. In order to compute daily maximum and minimum values of UTCI with the available data, the following approach has been implemented: Daily mean humidity, daily mean wind and daily maximum and minimum temperatures have been used from the CMIP5 daily data on single levels dataset (1971-2100). The solar and thermal radiative components of the UTCI are combined and represented in one single variable, the mean radiant temperature (MRT) before computing UTCI fields (DiNapoli et al. As all the mentioned aspects highly affect the temperature perceived by the human body and its ability to maintain its core temperature within certain boundaries in respect to external factors, they are therefore important to consider when investigating the effect of thermal stress on human health and people behaviour, making UTCI more accurate compared to the indexes considering only the temperature itself.
